{{Short description|1623 hymn tune}} {{Use mdy dates|date=April 2017}} {{Infobox musical composition | name = "Lasst uns erfreuen" | type = German [[hymn tune]] | composer = | image = LasstUnsErfreuen1625.jpg | alt = | caption = Oldest existing copy, 1625<ref>{{cite book |url=https://hymnsocietygbi.org.uk/1981/01/12/treasure-no-46-the-tune-lasst-uns-erfreuen-as-we-know-it/ |title=Catholische Kirchen Gesäng |language=de |location=Cologne |year=1625 |page=232 |access-date=April 7, 2017}}</ref> | native_name_lang = de | translation = Let us rejoice | text = | written = | based_on = | published = [[Cologne]], 1623 | meter = 88.88 with Alleluias | misc = [[File:Lasst uns erfreuen herzlich sehr.mid|center]]Original 1623 placement of the "Alleluia" phrases }} "'''{{lang|de|Lasst uns erfreuen herzlich sehr|italic=no}}'''" (Let us rejoice most heartily) is a [[hymn tune]] that originated from Germany in 1623, and which found widespread popularity after ''[[The English Hymnal]]'' published a 1906 version in strong [[triple meter]] with new lyrics. The triumphant melody and repeated "[[Alleluia]]" phrases have supported the tune's widespread usage during the [[Easter]] season and other festive occasions, especially with the English texts "[[Ye Watchers and Ye Holy Ones]]" and "[[All Creatures of Our God and King]]". <nowiki>''</nowiki>''Lasst uns erfreuen<nowiki>''</nowiki>'' derives its opening line and several other melodic ideas from ''GENEVAN 68'', which was initially published in a Lutheran service in 1525 as a setting for Psalm 119.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tune: LASST UNS ERFREUEN |url=https://hymnary.org/tune/lasst_uns_erfreuen |access-date=2024-12-02 |website=Hymnary.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Tune: OLD 113TH |url=https://hymnary.org/tune/old_113th_greiter |access-date=2024-12-02 |website=Hymnary.org |language=en}}</ref>
The tune's first known appearance was in the 1623 hymnal {{lang|de|Auserlesene, Catholische, Geistliche Kirchengesäng}} (Selected Catholic Spiritual Church-Songs) during the [[Counter-Reformation]] and the [[Thirty Years' War]], and the oldest published version that still exists is from 1625. The original 1623 hymnal was edited by [[Friedrich Spee]], an influential [[Jesuit]] priest, professor, and [[polemic|polemicist]] against [[witch-hunt]]s, who is often credited as the [[hymn]]'s composer and original lyricist.{{citation needed | date=January 2020|reason=Please cite some sources that credit this hymn to Spee. Have not seen this information elsewhere.}} ''The English Hymnal'' of 1906 was edited by [[Ralph Vaughan Williams]], whose arrangement of the hymn has become the standard for English-speaking churches.<ref name=treasure>{{cite journal |url=https://hymnsocietygbi.org.uk/1981/01/12/treasure-no-46-the-tune-lasst-uns-erfreuen-as-we-know-it/ |title=Treasure No 46: The Tune 'Lasst uns erfreuen' as we know it |first=John |last=Wilson |journal=Bulletin of the Hymn Society of Great Britain and Ireland |volume=IX.10 |issue=150 |date=Winter 1980 |access-date=April 7, 2017 |quote=One of the great successes of ''The English Hymnal'' in 1906 was its inclusion of the old German Catholic tune 'Lasst uns erfreuen', linked originally with Easter rejoicing, but now set to 'Ye watchers and ye holy ones', a new text by Athelstan Riley... The ''EH'' attribution of the melody was to the book ''[Auserlesene, Catholische,] Geistliche Kirchengesäng'' (Cöln, 1623)...}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Music and the Jesuit 'Way of Proceeding' in the German Counter-Reformation |first=Alexander J. |last=Fisher |journal=Journal of Jesuit Studies |volume=3 |issue=3 |pages=377–397 |year=2016 |doi=10.1163/22141332-00303003 |quote=Friedrich Spee, ''Auserlesene, Catholische, Geistliche Kirchengesäng'' (Cologne: Peter Brachel, 1623). Now lost, its contents have been reconstructed by Theo G. M. van Oorschot, in Spee, ''Sämtliche Schriften'' 4 (Tübingen: A. Francke, 2005).|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="HymnaryTunes">{{cite web |title=Lasst uns erfreuen |url=http://www.hymnary.org/tune/lasst_uns_erfreuen |access-date=April 7, 2017 |publisher=[[Hymnary.org]] |quote=Source: ''Auserlesen Catholische Geistliche Kirchengesäng'', Cologne, 1623. Scores: ... All Creatures of Our God and King ... Sing Hallelujah! Praise the LORD! ... Ye Watchers and Ye Holy Ones ... Praise God From Whom All Blessings Flow}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gp1GMTaUuzwC |first=Friedrich |last=Spee von Langenfeld |title=Cautio Criminalis, or a Book on Witch Trials |chapter=Translator's Introduction |translator-first=Marcus |translator-last=Hellyer |publisher=University of Virginia Press |isbn=978-0-8139-2182-2 |pages=vii, xi |year=2003 |orig-year=orig. 1631 |access-date=April 7, 2017 |quote=''Cautio Criminalis'' ... argued that the plague of witches supposedly infesting Germany was the product of the trials themselves and urged princes to supervise trials closely, to regulate the use of torture strictly, and even to end witch trials entirely. Although the book appeared anonymously, its author was immediately identified as Friedrich Spee, a forty-year-old Jesuit priest and professor of moral theology... He wrote many devotional songs, of which around a hundred appeared anonymously in collections of hymns between 1621 and 1637.}}</ref>

==Melody== In its original 1623 publication (of which no copies are now known to exist), "Lasst uns erfreuen" consisted of four eight-note text phrases, each immediately followed by a four-note Alleluia phrase, all of which was followed by the final triple-Alleluia refrain. In the earliest surviving copy of the hymn, in a 1625 collection, the hymn was restructured so that before the final refrain the eight-note text phrases occur in two pairs. The 1623 sequence is still common in German-language Catholic hymnals, while the 1625 version is more usual in English-language hymnals.<ref name=treasure/>
The verse consists of two repeated musical phrases with matching rhythms ("V", "v"), one using the upper pitches of the [[major scale]] and one using the lower pitches, and likewise for the Alleluia refrain ("R", "r"). Schematically, the structure of the original 1623 version can be represented as "vRvR VrVr RRr", and the revised 1625 sequence is "vvRR VVrr RRr", the tune thus achieving a "full and satisfying effect [built] with rare musical economy".<ref name=treasure/>

==Hymn texts== Below is the first verse from the original German (the 1625 publication, excluding the Alleluias), alongside a [[half-rhyme]]d, line-by-line English translation that shares the same 88.88 "[[long meter]]": {{verse translation |lang=de |Last uns erfrewen hertzlich sehr<!-- , Alleluia, Alleluia -->. Maria seufftzt und weint nicht mehr<!-- , Alleluia, Alleluia -->. Verschwunden alle Nebel sein<!-- , Alleluia, Alleluia -->. Jetzt scheint der lieben Sonnenschein<!-- , Alleluia, Alleluia -->. <!-- , Alleluia, Alleluia, Alleluia. --> | Let us most heartily rejoice. Maria sighs and weeps no more. All hazes now must disappear. The lovely shining sun now gleams. }} The original hymn still appears in the main German-language Catholic hymnal ''[[Gotteslob]]'', with slightly modernized text,<ref>{{cite book |url=https://www.carusmedia.com/images-intern/medien/00/0216100/0216100x.pdf |title=Gotteslob |chapter=533: Lasst uns erfreuen herzlich sehr, Halleluja |publisher=Carus |year=2013 |access-date=May 10, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.katholisch.de/video/14612-gotteslobvideo-gl-533-lasst-uns-erfreuen-herzlich-sehr-halleluja |work=Gotteslobvideo |title=GL 533: Lasst uns erfreuen herzlich sehr, Halleluja |publisher=katholisch.de |access-date=May 10, 2017 |quote=sung by the girls' and boys' choirs at Speyer Cathedral.}}</ref> and the tune as well in the Protestant ''[[Evangelisches Gesangbuch]]'' (Nr. 514) with a translation by Karl Budde (1929) of Draper's "All Creatures".
Especially since the early 1900s, versions of the tune have been used for many denominations, languages, and hymn texts.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hymnary.org/texts?qu=tuneAuthNumber%3Alasst_uns_erfreuen%20in%3Atexts |title=Text Results: Lasst uns erfreuen |publisher=Hymnary.org |access-date=April 7, 2017 |quote=Showing 1–49 of 49}}</ref> Some of these alternate texts are particularly notable, including alphabetically: <!-- Editors: Please include only hymns whose notability is established by reliable sources in "blue-linked" English Wikipedia articles, consistent with [[WP:CSC]] (Common Selection Criteria). --> * "[[All Creatures of Our God and King]]",<ref name=HymnaryTunes/> a paraphrase of [[Canticle of the Sun]] – by [[William Henry Draper (hymnwriter)|William Henry Draper]], in 1919. ** Adapted for festival choir, brass, percussion and organ<ref>{{cite book |url=https://global.oup.com/academic/product/all-creatures-of-our-god-and-king-9780193870406 |title=All Creatures of our God and King |first=John |last=Rutter |date=October 18, 2007 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-387040-6 |access-date=April 18, 2017}}</ref> – by [[John Rutter]], published 1974. * "Creator Spirit, by Whose Aid",<ref>{{cite web |url=http://cdn.ocp.org/shared/pdf/preview/22129z4.pdf |title=Creator Spirit, By Whose Aid |publisher=[[Oregon Catholic Press]] |access-date=May 9, 2017}}</ref> a paraphrase of [[Veni Creator Spiritus]] – by [[John Dryden]], published 1693. * "[[Doxology#"Praise God, from whom all blessings flow"|Praise God, from whom all blessings flow]]",<ref name=HymnaryTunes/> the [[Common Doxology]] – by [[Thomas Ken]], written 1674. * "Sing Hallelujah! Praise the L<small>ORD</small>!",<ref name="HymnaryTunes" /> an adaptation of [[Psalm 150]] – published in the Trinity Psalter Hymnal (Presbyterian) in 2018. * "[[Ye Watchers and Ye Holy Ones]]",<ref name=HymnaryTunes/> or {{lang|la|Vigiles et Sancti}} in Latin – by [[Athelstan Riley]], in a musical arrangement by [[Ralph Vaughan Williams]], published in ''[[The English Hymnal]]'' in 1906.<ref>''The English Hymnal'' (1906).London: Oxford University Press. #519.</ref> ** Adapted for the final movement of ''[[The Company of Heaven]]'',<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.allmusic.com/album/britten-the-company-of-heaven-mw0001850220 |access-date=April 16, 2017 |publisher=[[AllMusic]] |title=Britten: The Company of Heaven |quote=Sample... XI. Ye watchers and ye holy ones}}</ref> a cantata – by [[Benjamin Britten]], composed and published in 1937.
